title: Masked Menace Swings Over Midtown at Rush Hour
excerpt: Commuters on 42nd Street looked up to see the red-and-blue vigilante cut across six lanes of traffic. Was it heroics or a stunt?
author: Betty Brant
body: Shortly after 5:30 p.m. on Monday, hundreds of commuters on 42nd Street stopped in their tracks as a figure in a red-and-blue suit swung between office towers just above the evening traffic.

Witnesses say the masked figure caught a runaway delivery cart that had rolled off a loading dock and was heading for a crowded crosswalk. "It happened in two seconds," said Rosa Delgado, a nurse heading home from her shift. "One moment the cart was flying, the next it was stuck to a lamppost."

Not everyone was impressed. Traffic slowed to a crawl for nearly twenty minutes as drivers pulled over to film the scene, and the Department of Transportation confirmed it received more than forty complaints about the delay.
This newspaper has asked before and will ask again: who gave this masked individual permission to police our streets? Until someone answers that question, the Bugle will keep watching the skies.

title: Jewelry Heist Foiled on Fifth Avenue
excerpt: Three suspects were found wrapped in sticky webbing outside a jewelry store just before dawn, with the stolen goods sitting beside them.
author: Ben Ulrich
body: Police responding to a silent alarm at a Fifth Avenue jeweler early Saturday morning found three men suspended a few feet off the sidewalk, wrapped in what officers described as "an industrial amount of webbing."
A bag containing an estimated $2 million in watches and necklaces was found neatly placed by the store's front door, along with a hand-written note that read simply: "You're welcome."

The NYPD declined to comment on the vigilante's involvement but confirmed that all three suspects have been charged with burglary. A spokesperson reminded the public that "citizens should call 911 rather than take matters into their own hands."
Store owner Martin Feld said he was grateful but uneasy. "I'm happy the jewelry is back. I'm less happy that someone was crawling on my building at four in the morning."

title: City Council Debates Vigilante Registration Act
excerpt: A new bill would require anyone who fights crime in a mask to register with City Hall. Supporters call it common sense; critics call it unworkable.
author: Ned Leeds
body: The City Council held its first public hearing on Wednesday for the proposed Vigilante Registration Act, which would require masked crime fighters to file their real names with a new city office.

Councilmember Diane Okafor, the bill's sponsor, argued that the city cannot keep relying on people it cannot hold accountable. "If you damage a building or a car, someone has to pay for it. Right now, nobody does," she said.

Opponents questioned how the law could ever be enforced. "You are asking people whose whole strategy is staying anonymous to fill out a form," said civil liberties attorney Marcus Webb. "Good luck with that."
The council is expected to vote on the bill next month. The mayor's office has not said whether the mayor would sign it.

title: What Is the Web Made Of? Scientists Weigh In
excerpt: Researchers at Empire State University tested a sample left behind after a rooftop chase. Their findings raise more questions than answers.
author: Dr. Lena Choi
body: A small sample of webbing collected from a Queens rooftop last month has been analysed by a materials lab at Empire State University, and the results have surprised the team.

"Pound for pound, it is stronger than steel and stretches like rubber," said lab director Dr. Amir Haddad. "We have seen synthetic fibres with one of those properties. We have never seen one with both."

Even stranger, the sample dissolved completely within about two hours of being collected, leaving almost nothing to study. The team believes this is deliberate, so the material does not litter the city.
Dr. Haddad said his lab would welcome a fresh sample, "ideally handed over in person, with an explanation."

title: Editorial: A Hero Does Not Hide His Face
excerpt: Real heroes wear badges and name tags. This city deserves to know who is swinging over its rooftops, and why.
author: J. Jonah Jameson
body: Firefighters wear name tags. Police officers wear badges with numbers on them. Paramedics sign their reports. Every person we trust to keep us safe agrees to be held responsible for what they do.
So why should the masked menace be any different? He swings through our skyline, ties up suspects without a warrant and leaves property damage behind him, and then he disappears.
This newspaper does not doubt that some of his actions have helped people. But helping people does not put anyone above the rules the rest of us live by.
Take off the mask. Then we can talk about calling you a hero.

title: Queens Teens Start a Neighbourhood Watch in Red and Blue
excerpt: A group of high school students in Forest Hills has started patrolling their blocks in homemade costumes. Their parents are not thrilled.
author: Betty Brant
body: Every Friday evening, a group of about a dozen teenagers in red-and-blue hoodies walks the streets of Forest Hills, Queens, carrying flashlights and a first-aid kit.
"We are not fighting anyone," said 16-year-old Priya Raman, who started the group. "We help people carry groceries, we report broken streetlights, and we walk people home if they ask. That's it."

Local police say the group has been helpful so far, but they have asked the teens to stay off fire escapes and rooftops. Several parents told the Bugle they only agreed after the group promised to always walk in pairs.
The group now has its own social media page, with more than three thousand followers.

title: Armored Truck Robbery Stopped on Brooklyn Bridge
excerpt: A daylight attempt to hijack a cash truck ended in a traffic jam, two arrests and a getaway car stuck to the bridge cables.
author: Ben Ulrich
body: Traffic on the Brooklyn Bridge came to a standstill on Thursday afternoon after a group of armed men tried to force an armored truck to stop halfway across the span.

According to the truck's driver, a masked figure dropped onto the roof of the getaway car within a minute of the attack starting. Moments later the car was pinned to the bridge's suspension cables by thick strands of webbing.
Two suspects were arrested at the scene. A third escaped on foot into Manhattan and is still being sought by police.
The bridge was closed in both directions for more than an hour while crews removed the webbing, which had largely dissolved by the time they arrived.

title: Rooftop Sightings Map Shows Where He's Seen Most
excerpt: We plotted every sighting reported to the Bugle tip line this year. The results point to one surprising borough.
author: Ned Leeds
body: Since January, readers have sent the Bugle tip line 1,214 reports of the masked vigilante. We checked each one for a date, a time and a location, and placed the 870 usable reports on a map of the city.

Manhattan leads, as expected, with 52 percent of sightings, most of them in Midtown and the Financial District. The surprise is Queens, which accounts for nearly 30 percent, far more than Brooklyn or the Bronx.
Sightings peak between 9 p.m. and midnight, and they drop sharply on weekday mornings, which has led some readers to suggest the vigilante has a day job or goes to school.
The Bugle will update the map every month. Send your sightings, with photos if you can, to our tip line.

title: How Safe Is Swinging? A Physicist Does the Math
excerpt: Swinging between skyscrapers puts huge forces on the body. We asked a physics professor how anyone could survive it.
author: Dr. Lena Choi
body: At the bottom of a swing between two Manhattan towers, a person could be travelling at more than 100 kilometres per hour. That is where the trouble starts, says physics professor Elena Vasquez.

"At the lowest point the rope, or web, has to hold your weight and also pull you around the curve," she explained. "For a big swing that can be four or five times your body weight. Most people would black out."
Professor Vasquez says the vigilante either has unusual strength and balance, or plans his swings very carefully to keep them short and shallow. "Probably both," she added.
Her advice to anyone thinking of trying it themselves is simple: "Don't."

title: Letters: Readers Split on the Masked Question
excerpt: Our mailbag overflowed after last week's editorial. Here is a selection of what you told us, for and against.
author: Robbie Robertson
body: Last week's editorial drew more letters than any piece we have published this year. We received 642, and readers were split almost exactly down the middle.
"He pulled my son out of a stalled subway car. I don't need to know his name to know he's a good person," wrote a reader from the Bronx.
Others agreed with the editorial. "Nobody voted for him and nobody can fire him. That should worry all of us," wrote a retired judge from Staten Island.
We thank everyone who wrote in. The debate is clearly far from over, and our letters page remains open.
